articles.title: US trade chief to consider trade deal tariff caps in excess capacity probe - The Business Times
articles.summary: US trade chief to consider trade deal tariff caps in excess capacity probe  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
China’s excess production capacity and over-reliance on exports for growth is under scrutiny
[MILWAUKEE] US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Tuesday (Sep 29) that the Trump administration will take into consideration tariff caps negotiated in trade deals with countries as it weighs potential new duties in an investigation on excess industrial capacity.
Speaking to reporters ahead of a Group of 20 trade ministers meeting, Greer said he did not want to prejudge the outcome of a pending Section 301 investigation that is expected to focus on excess capacity in China and other key trading partners.
“I don’t want to get ahead of the report and proposed action, but I guess what I’ll say on that is we value those deals, and we will certainly take them into account when we’re looking at any outcomes of that report,” Greer said.
“What I will say as well is that a lot of those deals, they actually, you know, as they’re implemented, they go a long way to mitigating some of the impacts of excess capacity that might be present in those countries,” Greer said after a roundtable of CEOs and trade ministers.
The Trump administration has used its presidency of the G20 summit process this year to bring attention to China’s excess production capacity and over-reliance on exports for growth.
At the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, at the beginning of September, all G20 member countries except China agreed to take actions against such policies.
European Union trade chief Maros Sefcovic told the CEO roundtable on Tuesday he welcomed the Trump administration’s focus on combating excess industrial capacity at the G20 meeting.
Sefcovic said the EU was pushing for reforms on excess capacity in the G20 framework and at the World Trade Organization.
He also said the EU was working towards deeper cooperation with the US and other allies on critical minerals to secure supply chains and avoid “weaponisation” of the materials, production of which is currently dominated by China. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: The US Is Badly Losing Its Trade War with China - Cato Institute
articles.summary: The US Is Badly Losing Its Trade War with China  Cato Institute
articles.full_text:
Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House on Thursday will be the first Chinese state visit to the United States since 2015. It thus makes for the perfect time to judge the radical changes to US-China trade policy that President Donald Trump unleashed in 2018. After eight years of historically high tariffs, export controls, industrial policy, and more, we can conclude the policy has been a failure by its own objectives.
In March 2018, the US’s opening tariff salvo – implemented via Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 – aimed to roll back Chinese industrial policy and blunt Beijing’s push for dominance in advanced manufacturing. Subsequent tariffs and export controls added more goals: shrink China’s trade surplus and policy-driven overcapacity, reduce US dependence on Chinese goods, slow China’s technological advance, and weaken Beijing’s geopolitical position.
Granted, there have been a few superficial victories. Between 2017 and 2025, direct imports from China declined from about 21.6% of US goods imports in 2017 to roughly 9% by 2025, a level not seen since China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001. Export restrictions have denied Chinese companies easy access to Nvidia Corp.’s best chips and ASML Holding NV’s best chipmaking equipment. And American firms such as Apple Inc. shifted production capacity from China to India, Vietnam, Mexico, and other low-wage alternatives.
Beneath the surface, however, there’s little for trade hawks to cheer. New research finds that Chinese content – either directly or lawfully embedded in third-country goods – has been entering the US at levels only modestly below those in 2017, confirming the anecdotal evidence. Illegal transshipment and customs fraud have also increased – another predictable result of high and complex US tariffs. The 2025–26 drop in China’s import share, meanwhile, is mainly owed to surging AI inputs from Mexico and Taiwan – goods that were never made in China to begin with.
Outside the US, China’s trade position has never been stronger. Its trade surplus in goods rose to a record $1.19 trillion last year and is on pace to meet or exceed that total in 2026, with substantial export gains in non-US markets and in advanced industries like electronic vehicles. China also remains the world’s top manufacturing nation and the largest producer and exporter of intermediate goods – both by large margins. Chinese firms have ramped up both sales to and outbound investment in third-country production hubs facing lower US tariffs. Overall, Chinese exporters responded to new trade barriers not by shrinking but simply going around them.
China’s state capitalist economic model is also unchanged and may have been further entrenched by the US’s confrontational approach. In 2021, Beijing responded to US tariffs with a five-year plan that doubled down on industrial policy and technological self-reliance. According to the US-China Business Council, Beijing’s latest (15th) plan “suggests that industrial policy is no longer just one policy area among many but rather an organizing logic for the whole economy.”
Today, policymakers in Europe and elsewhere worry aloud about a destabilizing wave of Chinese exports – a “China Shock 2.0” – fueled by massive Chinese subsidies. State-owned enterprises, meanwhile, continue to play a large role in China’s economy and trade. Per the Peterson Institute, companies with full or substantial government ownership still accounted for 60% of the combined market value of China’s top 100 listed firms. American farm export targets in the most recent US-China trade deal perversely depend on state-owned Sinograin and COFCO.
American policy has proven ineffective – if not counterproductive – in other ways, too. Following the shock of US tariffs and export restrictions during Trump’s first term, Beijing worked to reduce its vulnerability to economic pressure from Washington and to develop asymmetric countermeasures should US coercion reemerge. This deepened Beijing’s involvement in China’s economy, led Chinese companies to look inward for technology and innovation, and gave the CCP new leverage – most notably over the rare earth minerals that US firms depend on – in bilateral talks. The moves help to explain why the 2018 wave of US tariffs produced a “Phase One” deal that (superficially, at least) favored Washington, while Trump’s second-term escalation has produced a stalemate.
Today, the US-China détente has, along with other Trump tariffs on non-China goods, so narrowed the gap between tariffs on Chinese imports and those on China alternative nations that some supply chains are now moving back into China. German firms are boosting their China investments while cutting US outlays. India has engaged with China after years of tension. And polls find China is viewed more favorably than the US in numerous countries for the first time.
American export controls and sanctions have also proven leaky. Research firm Epoch AI estimated that by the end of 2025 hundreds of thousands of Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips had reached China in violation of US export controls. Washington has relented on advanced chip sales to China, but no one there is buying because US restrictions prodded Chinese chipmakers to build passable alternatives. American firms, the Brookings Institute concluded in June, are now “shut out of the high end of the world’s largest chip market.”
These US policy failures don’t mean that China is an unstoppable hegemon in waiting. Beijing has set its lowest growth target in decades. Chinese technology still lags behind in certain advanced manufacturing industries, including top-end semiconductors. And the Chinese economy faces long-term headwinds – pervasive capital misallocation, sub-frontier productivity, smothering debt, and a rapidly aging population – that no amount of exports can fix.
But that’s very much the point. The problems in China’s economy are owed to factors beyond Washington’s control, and US trade restrictions since 2018 have done little to alter China’s trajectory while imposing a significant cost on American companies and consumers.
After eight years of failed unilateralism, Trump officials still don’t seem to understand that Washington can’t fundamentally change how the Chinese government organizes its economy, and that it’s better to focus US government efforts on a narrow set of real Chinese threats, on deepening non-China alliances, and on fixing American economic competitiveness across a range of issue areas.
Dramatic changes to Chinese policy must come from Chinese officials. Washington unfortunately keeps giving them reasons not to change.

articles.title: Will Brazil's New Critical Minerals Law Reshape Global Rare Earth Supply Chains? - ChemAnalyst
articles.summary: Will Brazil's New Critical Minerals Law Reshape Global Rare Earth Supply Chains?  ChemAnalyst
articles.full_text:
Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	Brazil's critical minerals sector entered a transformative phase in September 2026, as landmark federal legislation took effect and major corporate consolidations reshaped the competitive landscape. These developments position Brazil as an increasingly important alternative supplier for Western industrial chains seeking to reduce dependence on China, though regulatory clarity and project execution remain critical to realizing the country's geological potential.
	President Lula signed Law No. 15.506/2026 on 16 September, establishing the National Policy for Critical and Strategic Minerals (PNMCE) and creating the National Council for the Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE), linked directly to the presidency. The law prioritizes domestic processing over raw material exports and empowers CIMCE to scrutinize changes in corporate control, significant foreign influence, and international supply agreements affecting Brazil's economic or geopolitical security. It may also tie exports to value-addition commitments and require disclosure of destination, final beneficiary and degree of processing.
	The policy pairs oversight with incentives, including a R$2 billion Mineral Activity Guarantee Fund and tax credits of up to R$1 billion annually from 2030 to 2034. Companies must invest 0.3% of gross operating revenue in research and innovation, rising to 0.5% after six years. BNDES and Finep financing are also available. "The goal is precisely to transform the country's mineral potential into economic, technological and industrial development," the Ministry of Mines and Energy stated. Exactly which transactions fall under the new rules will depend on regulations issued after the law takes effect.
	The regulatory debate is not theoretical. US-based Rare Earth completed its combination with Serra Verde Group on 4 September, following an April agreement valued at approximately $2.8 billion. The deal creates a fully integrated Western rare earth platform spanning the Pela Ema mine in Goiás, the Round Top deposit in Texas, and Less Common Metals in the UK, alongside magnet manufacturing in Stillwater, Oklahoma. Serra Verde is the only large-scale producer outside Asia of all four magnetic rare earths—neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium—making Pela Ema strategically significant for Western supply diversification. However, the deal drew concern inside Brazil's government because Serra Verde's 15-year offtake commits first-stage mixed rare earth carbonate abroad, while Brasília wants domestic separation capacity. At the time the transaction was agreed, the government lacked the specific investment-screening mechanism now contemplated.
	Beyond Serra Verde, several foreign-listed companies are also developing major rare earth projects in Brazil. Australia-listed Viridis Mining and Minerals is advancing the Colossus ionic-adsorption clay project in Minas Gerais, while Meteoric Resources and St George Mining are developing the Caldeira and Araxá projects.
	Meanwhile, Brazilian Rare Earths (BRE) has started its Stage I metallurgical pilot plant in Camaçari, Bahia. The company also secured R$6.4 million in funding for a Stage II hydrometallurgical plant, which is expected to produce NdPr oxide, heavy rare earth concentrate, and uranium yellowcake when it starts operations in Q2 2027. French separation specialist Carester will lead the separation work and become an offtake partner for heavy rare earth products.
	In contrast to rare earth progress, Sigma Lithium's Grota do Cirilo mine faced a full suspension of environmental permits by a Minas Gerais federal court following a lawsuit from the Federation of Quilombola Communities. The court found that the mine's distance from the Baú Quilombola community fell within the 8-kilometer threshold requiring free, prior and informed consultation. The ruling halts all mining and processing at Brazil's largest lithium operation, which had already faced repeated interruptions in 2023, January 2026 and July 2026.
Foreign miners, governments and industrial groups are already positioning themselves around Brazil's deposits. The next test is whether Brasília can accelerate investment without deterring the capital it needs, while ensuring more processing and industrial value remains in Brazil. For procurement-focused readers, Brazil's emergence as a Western-aligned supplier of rare earths and critical minerals is worth monitoring, though the timeline for large-scale separation and metal production capacity remains contingent on regulatory clarity and project execution.

articles.title: What is Section 301? Why EAM Jaishankar says US trade probe could impact the deal - dailyhunt.in
articles.summary: What is Section 301? Why EAM Jaishankar says US trade probe could impact the deal  dailyhunt.in
articles.full_text:
India-US trade deal talks have moved close to an agreement, but an ongoing US trade investigation under Section 301 could still influence when the two countries formally conclude the pact, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has said.
Speaking at a special interaction hosted by the Asia Society, EAM Jaishankar said negotiations had reached a broad understanding, but the continuing Section 301 process remained an important factor in deciding when to finalise the agreement.
"The 301 process is still in the works, it's still unfolding. So the issue for us is at what point do you close out an agreement which is very, very far advanced," he noted.
What is Section 301?
Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 allows Washington DC to investigate foreign trade practices it considers unfair or burdensome to US commerce.
The Office of the US Trade Representative, or USTR, conducts these investigations and can recommend or impose measures including additional tariffs and other trade restrictions.
The provision gives Donald trump administered- US a mechanism to respond to foreign trade practices outside the normal tariff negotiations conducted through bilateral agreements.
For India, the current Section 301 process has become relevant because it could affect the tariff environment facing Indian exporters in US market.
Why is Section 301 important for India?
In June 2026, the USTR examined 60 economies over forced-labour-related import restrictions and enforcement practices, including India.
The initial proposal for India was an additional 12.5 per cent tariff. Following engagement between New Delhi and Washington DC, the final additional tariff was reduced to 10 per cent in July 2026.
The lower rate was viewed by India's Commerce Ministry as the result of sustained engagement with the US and changes to India's policy aimed at preventing imports linked to forced labour.
However, the broader Section 301 process is still unfolding. That uncertainty is now relevant to the timing of the India-US trade agreement.
India-US trade deal is 'very, very far advanced'
Jaishankar also explained why negotiations have taken longer than initially expected, pointing to differences between the structures of the Indian and US economies.
"India is a society of small producers, small agriculture producers, small factories. So the, you know, apart from the per capita gap between India and the United States, the nature of production, nature of society is very different. So a trade negotiation required a certain amount of, I think, of patience and detailing to see it through," he said.
Jaishankar said expectations of a rapid agreement had been tested by the complexity of the negotiations.
"...expectation that it could rapidly move forward, I think, was tested against a ground reality which was much more complex. So, today, I think we have reached a situation where there is more or less an understanding on the trade agreement."
Why tariff competitiveness matters for India
The final tariff structure is important for Indian exporters competing with suppliers from ASEAN, China and Bangladesh in the US market.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal had earlier described the bilateral trade pact as "done and dusted", while saying it could move forward once India secures appropriate competitive advantages in the US market relative to regional competitors.
For businesses, the eventual agreement could influence export costs, market access and investment decisions. The Section 301 process adds another variable because any additional US trade measures could alter the competitive environment even as the bilateral pact approaches completion.

articles.title: How Chinese capital is flowing into Vietnam amid tariff pressure - Theinvestor
articles.summary: How Chinese capital is flowing into Vietnam amid tariff pressure  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Recent disclosures show some Chinese companies expanding production in Vietnam to serve North American and European markets while reducing exposure to tariff risks. The investment is moving beyond new factories, with projects beginning to translate into production capacity and international orders.
Shanghai CIG Tech, a manufacturer of telecommunications and optoelectronic equipment, said in a disclosure at the end of August that production lines at its Vietnam facility had passed customer assessments and certifications and had begun operations.
The company expects Vietnam to become an important production base in its overseas manufacturing network as output increases, helping reduce costs and improve access to customers.
In a recent report, Minbao Photoelectric, a lighting equipment manufacturer, had previously planned to put its Vietnam factory into operation from August 2026, with annual output value estimated at about 500 million yuan ($74.51 million) at full capacity. However, the company's disclosure at the end of August said the project was still under construction.
According to the company, production capacity in Vietnam is being established to support its expansion in North America while responding to the risk of greater protectionism in Europe. In an earlier disclosure, the company also said its Vietnam facility would help reduce the impact of tariff policies and better serve North American customers.
The moves come as Vietnam and the United States draw closer to a final outcome in their trade deal negotiations. At a meeting in New York on September 21, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the two sides had made significant progress and were very close to a final outcome on a reciprocal, fair and balanced trade agreement.
U.S.-China trade tensions have also eased from earlier rounds of tariff confrontation, with the two sides continuing to expand cooperation in some less-sensitive product categories. On September 27, the USTR said the United States and China had proposed about $30 billion worth of goods from each side that could receive more favorable trading conditions under a new dialogue mechanism.
However, trade relations between the world's two largest economies have yet to return to normal. The current tariff truce remains temporary, while differences over technology, market access and enforcement of trade commitments have not been fully resolved.
Chinese FDI into Vietnam rises
A study published by U.S. Federal Reserve researchers in July found that after the United States raised tariffs on Chinese goods in 2018-2019, Chinese companies played a significantly larger role in exports from Vietnam to the United States.
According to the Fed, Chinese-invested companies accounted for about 11% of Vietnam's goods exports to the United States in 2018-2019. That share rose to 25% in 2020-2023, while the share from Vietnamese companies fell from about 33% to 23%.
Notably, the Fed excluded transactions involving goods routed through Vietnam to the U.S. market. One example would be a company importing a product from China and exporting it to the United States under the same product code within the same quarter.
The study also found that new foreign-invested companies established in Vietnam after 2018 tended to be more dependent on the U.S. market and used more intermediate goods from China than companies that had already been operating in Vietnam before that period.
The approach was intended to limit the inclusion in Vietnam's exports of Chinese goods passing through Vietnam without clear evidence of production activity there.
This suggests tariffs can change where some stages of production are located without necessarily causing supply chains to shift away from China. A factory can move to Vietnam while some raw materials and components continue to come from China.
The new investment project data used by the Fed showed that Chinese investment in Vietnam increased sharply after 2018, particularly in manufacturing and industrial goods. The trend has continued in investment flows in 2026.
According to Vietnam's Foreign Investment Agency, total registered capital from mainland Chinese investors, including new investment, additional capital and capital contributions and share purchases, reached about $3.69 billion in the first seven months of the year, up 31.5% from a year earlier and ranking fourth among investors in Vietnam.
More notably, China ranked first by the number of newly registered projects, with 849 projects, accounting for 35% of all new foreign-invested projects during the period. It ranked first in capital contribution and share purchase transactions, with 494 deals.
By the end of August, according to the National Statistics Office, newly registered capital from mainland China alone stood at about $1.93 billion, accounting for 8.9% of total newly registered FDI in Vietnam and ranking fourth after Singapore, South Korea and Hong Kong.
The figures show that China is not yet the largest investor in Vietnam by capital value, but has a significant presence in terms of the number of projects. The next question is what those projects are doing after the factories are built, and which stages of the production chain are being carried out by workers in Vietnam.
From investment to production capacity and orders
Guizhou Tyre is an example of the scale involved. According to the company's official website, the third phase of its Vietnam plant represents total investment of about $228 million and has a designed capacity of 6 million radial tyres a year.
The first tyre rolled off the production line in July 2025. The company said products from the project are intended for more than 100 countries and territories, including Europe, North America, Southeast Asia and Brazil.
This suggests production is not limited to assembly or packaging, as may have been the case previously, but can include finished goods manufactured in Vietnam using locally sourced inputs such as natural rubber.
If Guizhou Tyre illustrates the scale of production, Supor provides a clearer example of the shift in orders.
According to company information, during a meeting with investors on April 24, its Vietnam operation was handling most of Supor's orders for the North American market, mainly cookware. The Chinese home-appliance maker also said it would adjust production capacity in Vietnam according to market demand, international trade developments and changes in tariff policies.
Another mechanism can be seen at Jingyan Technology. According to the company, it has allocated part of its production capacity for metal injection moulding components to Vietnam.
Notably, some major customers have required the company to establish production capacity in Vietnam to meet product-origin requirements.
This case shows that the decision to move part of production capacity outside China may not come solely from manufacturers, but can also be driven by requirements from customers within the supply chain.
In ceramics, Huaci said in an early September disclosure that the first phase of its Vietnam facility was expected to generate output worth about 300 million to 400 million yuan ($59.61 million), with two production lines, one of which would supply IKEA.
The company said ceramic products made in China face an anti-dumping duty of 79% when entering Europe, while its Vietnam facility enjoys more favorable tariff conditions, allowing it to regain some export orders that had previously been difficult to fulfil from China.
These cases show a deeper chain following the flow of capital: factories are built, production lines are approved by customers, capacity increases and, ultimately, international orders are brought to Vietnam.
However, locating a factory in Vietnam does not automatically mean a company can avoid tariff barriers.
A precedent has emerged in the solar-panel industry. The U.S. Commerce Department has previously determined that some products completed in Vietnam using Chinese components underwent only limited processing before being exported to the United States and were therefore subject to anti-dumping and countervailing duties applicable to Chinese goods.
In that investigation, Vina Solar, which operates a factory in Van Trung Industrial Park in Bac Ninh province, was found to have circumvented the duties. Boviet Solar, which operates a factory in Song Khe-Noi Hoang Industrial Park, also in Bac Ninh, was not found to have done so.
The different findings in the two cases show that the issue is not simply whether a factory is located in Vietnam, but also the origin of its inputs and the extent of actual production carried out there.
Under current U.S. rules, goods determined to have been transshipped to evade tariffs can face an additional 40% duty as well as other penalties.
The fact that Vietnam and the United States are moving closer to a final outcome in their trade deal negotiations is not enough to conclude that a new wave of Chinese investment will emerge. Most of the projects currently being developed were prepared earlier.
But as capital continues to flow in and some factories begin securing production capacity, customers and international orders, the next measure is no longer simply how much Chinese FDI Vietnam attracts, but how much actual production activity is being shifted there.

articles.title: Pearl Global: With Goldman Sachs Backing and Clients Like Zara & Calvin Klein, How Is It Building a Tariff-Proof Business? - Trade Brains
articles.summary: Pearl Global: With Goldman Sachs Backing and Clients Like Zara & Calvin Klein, How Is It Building a Tariff-Proof Business?  Trade Brains
articles.full_text:
The global apparel industry has been reshaped by rising tariffs, changing sourcing strategies and the growing need for retailers to diversify their supply chains. For Indian garment manufacturers, this has created both a challenge and an opportunity. Companies that depend heavily on one country for production can face a sharp impact when tariffs change, while those with a wider manufacturing network can shift orders across markets.
Pearl Global Industries is building its business around this flexibility. With manufacturing operations spread across India, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia and Guatemala, the company can move production closer to customers and adjust its sourcing mix when trade conditions change. Its relationships with global names such as Zara, Calvin Klein, Tommy Hilfiger, GAP and Walmart also give it a broad customer base.
With a market cap of Rs 12,000crore, the shares of Pearl Global Industries Ltd are trading at Rs 1,300 and are trading at a PE of 38 compared to their industry's PE of 27. The shares have given a return of more than 1,600% in the last 5 years.
Tariffs Changed the Game
The biggest challenge for Indian apparel exporters came after the US raised tariffs on products made in India. This was a problem because the US is a key market, and buyers can easily shift their sourcing to countries with lower tariffs. However, Pearl Global benefits from a manufacturing presence across geographies.
Management estimates that 15%-18% of consolidated revenues are related to exports into the United States from India. This aspect is significant, as it does not mean that all operations would depend on exports from India to the United States. Instead, this provides the company the option of servicing similar customers across different production facilities.
Five-Country Footprint'
The manufacturing locations of Pearl Global include five distinct geographic manufacturing locations, comprising about 25 manufacturing facilities, having the capacity to produce over 100 million pieces. India, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Guatemala each play their own unique role within Pearl Global's manufacturing and logistics operations.
This diversification acts as a protective measure for Pearl Global against the effects of tariffs. While Pearl Global cannot insulate itself entirely from the impact of tariffs through such diversification, the ability to manufacture based on customers' demands, product type, cost, and trade dynamics allows Pearl Global greater flexibility.
Guatemala Adds US Access
Why is Guatemala significant? The reason lies in the fact that Guatemala allows Pearl Global access to nearshoring in the United States market. According to Pearl Global's information literature prepared for investors, the firm views geographic proximity to the United States, reduced lead times and free trade into the US as key competitive benefits.
Clearly then, the factory represents more than just any standard manufacturing plant. It provides the capacity for the firm to cater to clients closer to home in the USA without having to rely entirely upon manufacturing in India. Pearl Global expects its Guatemala factory to break even by FY27.
Bangladesh Drives Scale
Bangladesh constitutes yet another critical element of the value chain. Pearl Global operates nine plants in the nation, capable of producing up to 60 million units. This constitutes one of the largest production bases within the group’s network. The types of products manufactured at these facilities include those belonging to the categories of woven, knit and denim products.
With the presence of a large-scale apparels ecosystem within Bangladesh, Pearl Global can produce considerable amounts for its international retail brands. The firm has been continuously increasing its manufacturing footprint within the nation, even building new capacities like laundry facilities. This creates a second major base for the group, which enables it to serve its international clients without being dependent solely on Indian-origin shipments.
Vietnam and Indonesia Add Flexibility
There is another aspect to the company's logistics network that lies in Vietnam. Vietnam has facilities that specialise in making items such as outerwear, jackets and puffies, but there are ongoing developments into the Indonesian market too. As part of the group's strategy, there would be a distribution of manufacture according to each country's manufacturing capacity and matching products to capabilities.
What becomes a key strategic point is the creation of a supply chain where manufacture will not be limited to one particular market. As international retailers begin to reassess logistics because of issues ranging from tariffs, geopolitics, transportation costs and delivery schedules, this kind of geographic diversification will prove to be critical for Pearl Global.
Global Brands Strengthen the Model
The customer base of Pearl Global includes prominent names like Zara, Calvin Klein, Tommy Hilfiger, Ralph Lauren, GAP, Old Navy, American Eagle, Levi's, Walmart, Target Australia, Primark and TJ Maxx. Its range of products includes knits, wovens, denims, outerwear and activewear.
This matters because fashion apparel manufacturing involves more than providing the cheapest solution. Leading retailers require dependable manufacturers who deliver reliable supply chains and have the capacity to meet their volume requirements. According to Pearl Globally, the company targets financially healthy customers with significant long-term strategic value, including AAA-rated customers. Such a strategy enables the creation of customer partnerships that lead to repeat business at multiple facilities.
Capacity Leaves Room to Grow
Pearl Global’s manufacturing capacity has grown steadily, exceeding 100 million pieces currently. The firm has announced additional capacity additions as part of its medium-term expansion strategy. The capacity at its India business alone stands close to 26 million pieces, and according to the management, even higher utilisation rates could possibly help achieve a substantial rise in revenue generation.
The opportunity appears particularly timely in India itself, considering Pearl Global’s own diversification into product segments including men’s wear and bottoms alongside geographical diversification into tier-2 & tier-3 regions in India.
Furthermore, Pearl Global has already positioned itself in anticipation of European orders, and several of its factories have already received certifications from Europe-bound customers. Thus, the firm seems well-placed in case international apparel companies decide to source diversification towards India.
Financials Show Resilience
Quarterly financial performance from Pearl Global reveals that the business continues to scale. Consolidated revenues for June, which is Q1 FY27, stood at Rs 1,528 crore compared to Rs 1,228 crore in June last year, marking a 24.5% growth year-on-year.
The operating profit was Rs 164 crore from Rs 112 crore previously, while the operating margin expanded to 11% from 9%. Profit before tax was Rs 120 crore from Rs 76 crore, while the net profit jumped by nearly 50% to Rs 99 crore from Rs 66 crore. EPS rose to Rs 10.88 from Rs 7.38.
Sequential quarterly trends are noteworthy too. Revenues grew from Rs 1,314 crore in March this year to Rs 1,528 crore in June, while operating profit went from Rs 134 crore to Rs 164 crore and net profit from Rs 81 crore to Rs 99 crore.
From Tariffs to Opportunity
Pearl Global's most significant competitive strength lies in its flexible global manufacturing base, which includes operations in India, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia and Guatemala. This structure makes it possible to shift the sourcing mix in response to changes in tariff rates, customer needs and global trade patterns. In this regard, the company's value proposition includes providing retail customers a diversified sourcing arrangement instead of relying solely on one nation's manufacturing base.
Goldman Sachs Funds – Goldman Sachs India Equity portfolio held a 1.68% stake as of September 2026, adding institutional interest to the story, although the holding should not be treated as an endorsement of the company's strategy.
In light of the trends currently emerging in the apparel industry concerning the repositioning of manufacturing and sourcing locations, Pearl Global appears well-placed to leverage this manufacturing network to capitalise on any opportunities created. Given its existing connections with international retail chains, diverse product range and access to different sources worldwide, it becomes possible to utilise supply chain diversification as an engine of growth.

articles.title: Prabowo Mobilizes State Capital and Tariff Shield to Rescue Indonesia’s $12B Textile Pillar - InvestorTrust
articles.summary: Prabowo Mobilizes State Capital and Tariff Shield to Rescue Indonesia’s $12B Textile Pillar  InvestorTrust
articles.full_text:
Prabowo Mobilizes State Capital and Tariff Shield to Rescue Indonesia’s $12B Textile Pillar
Key Takeaways
| ● | President Prabowo Subianto directed the cabinet to execute an overhaul of Indonesia’s textile and textile product (TPT) sector to safeguard four million jobs and protect $12 billion in annual exports. | 
| ● | Sovereign investment agency BPI Danantara will establish a new integrated upstream-to-downstream state-owned enterprise (BUMN) operating within a dedicated industrial hub to partner with domestic mills. | 
| ● | The administration instructed customs authorities to clamp down on illicit secondhand clothing and volume-dumped garments while reviewing technical import rules to ease raw material access for mills. | 
| ● | Jakarta is accelerating the Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (IEU-CEPA) toward 2026 ratification to eliminate trade barriers and expand duty-free garment shipments into Europe by early 2027. | 
JAKARTA, Investortrust.id — Confronted by cheap offshore dumping and mounting insolvencies across legacy factories, President Prabowo Subianto has launched an aggressive, state-led intervention to revitalize Indonesia’s textile and apparel industry—one of the archipelago’s largest manufacturing export earners and a cornerstone of blue-collar employment.
Chairing a limited cabinet meeting with senior economic ministers at the Presidential Palace in Jakarta on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, Prabowo ordered sweeping policy adjustments spanning tariff harmonizations, raw material deregulation, sovereign restructuring capital, and an expedited trade corridor into the European Union.
The stakes are critical for Southeast Asia’s largest economy. The textile and textile product (TPT) ecosystem represents approximately 0.97% of national gross domestic product (GDP), absorbs roughly 4 million factory workers, and generates $12 billion in annual export receipts. Ranking consistently among Indonesia’s most valuable non-commodity export lines, the sector has held strategic priority as a vital hedge against global commodity volatility.
"This is one of the most strategic labor-intensive sectors," Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto stated following the meeting on Tuesday. "In our briefing to the President, we conveyed that the textile and garment sector is growing above the baseline economic rate at 5.6%, while leather goods and footwear expanded by 8.25%."
Danantara Steps In: Building a New Integrated State Player
A centerpiece of the government's rescue strategy involves deploying sovereign investment fund Badan Pengelola Investasi Daya Anagata Nusantara (BPI Danantara). Rather than simply disbursing liquidity lines to debt-ridden manufacturers, Danantara will establish an entirely new state-owned enterprise (BUMN) designed to build an integrated supply chain from the ground up.
Chief Executive Officer of Danantara Rosan Perkasa Roeslani confirmed the move at the Presidential Palace on Tuesday evening, emphasizing that the state will directly spearhead midstream and downstream clustering.
"We will create a new company to support existing textile players, and we can partner with established textile companies," Rosan said on Tuesday. "However, for full integration, we will be the ones initiating it within a single consolidated zone."
Danantara Chief Operating Officer Dony Oskaria added that capital expenditure commitments and execution schedules remain under active internal review. Concurrently, Prabowo instructed Danantara and state-linked commercial lenders to immediately intervene in debt workouts for viable operators facing credit distress, dismissing perceptions that apparel manufacturing is an obsolete domestic industry.
"The President emphasized that the textile industry is not a sunset industry," Airlangga explained on Tuesday. "This clarity should encourage reinvestment and working capital expansion from the banking sector."
Closing the Smuggling Valve and Easing Mill Inputs
To restore domestic market margins, the administration is pairing state enterprise formation with aggressive market-defense measures. Factory floors have faced relentless pressure from unrecorded bulk imports, weight-based garment clearances, and illicit secondhand balepress shipments that undercut domestic price structures.
Prabowo instructed the Directorate General of Customs and Excise to escalate enforcement against illicit apparel trafficking. The mandate came directly alongside a broader review of Ministry of Industry technical import regulations (Pertek), aiming to dismantle bureaucratic red tape that has choked spinning and weaving mills of essential overseas fiber inputs.
Cabinet officials are also formulating regulatory accommodations to support seasonal labor dynamics. Under the proposed framework, authorities are exploring flexible short-term work contracts (PKWT) alongside selective exemptions or evaluations of value-added tax (PPN) charges for export-oriented apparel factories.
The European Trade Gateway: Accelerating IEU-CEPA
Beyond protecting the domestic perimeter, Jakarta is betting that opening premium Western consumer markets can structurally re-energize order books for Indonesian garments.
During the same cabinet session, Prabowo ordered his trade negotiators to finalize the legal text of the Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (IEU-CEPA). The bilateral pact is currently completing legal vetting in English before submission to the European Parliament, with Indonesian parliamentary ratification slated for late 2026 to enable full implementation in early 2027.
European Union Trade and Economic Security Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and top EU leaders are scheduled to visit Jakarta between late October and early November 2026 to formalize the landmark accord.
Securing duty-free access across Europe's 27 member nations is viewed by trade strategists as an essential catalyst. By eliminating import duties that previously left Indonesian apparel at a competitive disadvantage against rivals like Vietnam and Bangladesh, the trade pact aims to double Indonesian export shipments to Europe, ensuring that Southeast Asia’s historic garment powerhouse secures a durable foothold in global supply chains.

articles.title: US manufacturing revival gathers pace despite tariff and energy headwinds | articles - think.ing.com
articles.summary: US manufacturing revival gathers pace despite tariff and energy headwinds | articles  think.ing.com
articles.full_text:
After three years of stagnation, US manufacturing appears to be on an upswing as production and order books gain momentum. Tariffs and energy costs pose challenges, but trends in reshoring, AI/robotic technologies and rising defence spending provide reasons for longer-term optimism
The US manufacturing sector has experienced a torrid couple of decades. Output volumes remain 10% below the peak level hit just before the Global Financial Crisis in December 2007. The sector employs a million fewer workers than it did 20 years ago. Reasons for this poor performance include consumer demand preferences shifting ever further toward services over physical goods, underinvestment in advanced production facilities relative to international competitors, high US labour costs and the removal of trade barriers allowing foreign manufacturers to gain market share.
Nonetheless, the sector has shown genuine signs of a revival over the past year. The ISM production index has moved from sub-50 contraction territory to signalling robust growth ahead. Below, we look at what is driving this turnaround and how it could evolve.
Tariffs remain President Trump’s primary tool
Reviving manufacturing has been top of mind for all recent presidents. In his first term, President Trump’s solution was to impose tariffs on Chinese-made imports along with sector-specific levies. The rationale being that this would boost the price competitiveness of US manufacturers in key sectors. Yet it failed to generate the desired turnaround. Initiatives from President Biden similarly yielded little benefit.
In his second term, President Trump doubled down, initially announcing 25% tariffs on steel and aluminium, and then a 25% tariff on auto parts before launching into his 'Liberation Day' tariffs in April 2025 that dramatically expanded coverage.
Invoked under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), individual tariff rates changed based on a trading partner's willingness to open markets to US manufacturers and guarantee investment within the US. The chart below shows that the realised tariff rate undershot the calculated implied average tariff rate based on the full-year 2024 import mix.
Reasons for this include import substitution via switching to lower-tariffed foreign suppliers, a surge in tariff-exempt high-tech imports, and better USMCA compliance. This means a greater proportion of Canadian and Mexican trade qualified for tariff exemptions, and some modest evidence of switching towards US-made products.
The Supreme Court ruled against those tariffs in late February. In response, Trump swiftly invoked Section 122 of the 1974 Trade Act. It allows tariffs of up to 15% for as long as 150 days before the US Trade Representative launches Section 301 investigations. The end result is 10% tariffs on 14 countries, including the EU, Mexico, Canada and the UK, with 46 other countries, including imports from China, Japan and India facing a 12.5% tariff. This, in itself, is a lower tariff regime under the IEEPA system.
Given several important tech and medical categories are exempted, we expect the realised tariff rate to come close to 7%. This is a less onerous environment than 12 months ago. Moreover, importing companies' cash flows are being boosted by the Supreme Court’s decision to insist that the $166bn of IEEPA tariffs be fully refunded. That means the realised tariff rate temporarily fell into negative territory in July, as IEEPA refunds more than offset all other tariff charges.
Reshoring yet to show up in construction activity
Citing the effectiveness of tariffs, the Administration has touted the “largest reshoring wave in American history”. It points to a four-year high for the ISM manufacturing index while employment in the manufacturing sector rose 58,000 in the first eight months of this year. Amid pledges from corporate America to invest more in the US, the National Association of Manufacturers reported that foreign direct investment in US manufacturing reached a new record level in 2025 of $2.5tr.
Yet manufacturing-related construction activity does not reflect this positive narrative. Manufacturing construction spending peaked in September 2024 at an annualised $249bn and currently stands at $170bn. We’ve seen a sharp slowdown in construction activity in the computer, electronics and electrical sector from $126bn to $57bn over that same period. That follows the conclusion of the CHIPS and Science Act from the previous Biden Administration, which provided nearly $53bn to boost the domestic semiconductor industry. Strip out this sector and construction activity tied to the rest of manufacturing has changed little over the past two years. So, despite commitments from business leaders, little evidence suggests that a reshoring boom is underway just yet.
While tariffs may improve the relative cost comparison versus foreign products, the National Association of Manufacturers states that in 2024, manufacturing employees earned an average of $106,691, including pay and benefits. That is substantially higher than the average cost of employing someone in China, South Korea and even Germany. This suggests that for manufacturing reshoring to make sense, it would be tied to companies that are highly automated with high value-added production. Alternatively, there could be an appetite to reshore where consumers are willing to pay the premium for a 'Made in America' label or where security of supply chains is an imperative.
Sectors most likely to receive a boost include technology, transport and aerospace, electric vehicles, clean energy and pharmaceuticals. The latter is where we have seen the largest announcements, with Johnson & Johnson’s $55bn investment spending plan over the next four years and Eli Lilly announcing a $27bn investment in its US manufacturing operations. And in solar manufacturing, tariffs, price floors, and China-focussed trade restrictions are supporting the expansion of US manufacturing across the value chain.
While the construction numbers aren’t showing any uplift yet, it takes significant time to get planning in place. Advanced manufacturing plants also take a long time to construct. Intel, for example, suggests it takes three to five years with 6,000 construction workers at a cost of $10bn to build a new factory. An aluminium smelter takes two to three years for construction, in addition to the time needed to design and secure planning approval. Significant infrastructure is also typically required for all new manufacturing sites, including power, road, rail and water, adding to the cost of reshoring.
The Middle East conflict and energy prices
Restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have raised concerns about energy shortages, higher prices and potential production disruption for manufacturers globally. However, the US is better positioned to manage those challenges than European and Asian competitors. The US produces more energy than it consumes. Oil prices are set in global markets and push up the cost of gasoline and diesel, with freight costs consequently increasing in the US and elsewhere. However, the US is in a better position relative to foreign competitors in terms of natural gas. Abundant domestic production is keeping prices well below long-run averages.
This has a knock-on effect: lower electricity prices vis-à-vis other countries, which should give US manufacturers a cost advantage over foreign peers. US-based companies involved with steel, metal and glass production – heavy industries that require high-temperature processes – and agriculture and fertiliser production, which use natural gas to convert into nitrogen fertilisers, should be relative winners on the global stage. Similarly, the availability of natural gas, used as a feedstock to create products such as plastics, should give a competitive boost for US manufacturers.
Nevertheless, electricity-intensive manufacturers could come under pressure as AI-driven data centre growth drives up power demand. For example, Emirates Global Aluminium and Century Aluminium are planning a 750,000-ton aluminium smelter in Oklahoma, the first new US smelter in almost 50 years. The facility would double current US aluminium output, but may face challenges competing with data centres for power.
Financial conditions are a headwind
Borrowing costs have risen in response to elevated energy prices and a belief that the Federal Reserve is set to tighten policy and keep interest rates higher for longer. In an environment of substantial government fiscal deficits and anxiety about debt sustainability, US longer-dated Treasury yields have pushed above 5%. Corporate bond spreads have tightened, but not by enough to prevent an overall rise in borrowing costs. Moody’s 10Y Aaa corporate debt benchmark index is pointing to a 56bp increase in borrowing costs since the start of the year.
Mortgage rates, auto loans and credit card borrowing costs all increased for similar reasons. This will act as a brake on economic activity over time. Auto loan and credit card delinquencies are already on par with the rates recorded in the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis, and the household saving ratio is around 3pp below its long-run average of 6%. As such, this tightening of financial conditions, amplified by the recent strengthening of the US dollar, is a headwind for the sector.
Sector performance diverges markedly
Tariffs and energy security do boost the attractiveness of manufacturing in the US. But so does US economic growth continuing to outperform other key markets. Between 2023 and 2026, the US economy has grown an average of 2.5% year-on-year in volume terms versus 0.9% in Europe.
At the same time, the US Administration believes maintaining the lead in the AI/technology frontier is imperative for both economic and national security, given competition from China. Rapid AI adoption is leading to robust construction of data centres, boosting electricity demand and spur

articles.summary: CPTPP offers opportunities for supply-chain diversification amid global trade shifts  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNS/VNA) - The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) is increasingly becoming not simply as a market for selling goods, but as a platform to diversify suppliers, production networks and export destinations amid a restructuring of global trade. 
 
 Speaking at a seminar organised by Cong Thuong (Industry and Trade) Magazine on September 28, Ngo Chung Khanh, deputy director of the Multilateral Trade Policy Department under the Ministry of Industry and Trade, said changing trade policies are prompting countries and companies to reassess established supply chains. 
 
 “Relationships that were once considered very stable are becoming less so,” Khanh said, adding that differences in policies and trade positions were encouraging countries to seek alternative sources of supply. 
 
 Vietnam, with its position as a manufacturing hub in the region, could benefit from this shift as international companies look to diversify suppliers, he said. 
 
 The CPTPP, which currently comprises 12 economies, provides Vietnamese businesses with a broader framework for participating in those supply chains, Khanh said. The bloc is also expanding its reach, with countries Costa Rica and Uruguay seeking for membership, while other have expressed interest in joining. 
 
 Vietnam’s trade with CPTPP members still accounts for a modest share of their overall import demand, indicating significant room for expansion, Khanh said. 
 
 The opportunity extends beyond exports, he said. Companies can use CPTPP markets to source inputs, diversify suppliers and reorganise production networks to reduce dependence on a single source. 
 
 “CPTPP is not simply a consumer market. It is also a supply chain,” he said. 
 
 Market diversification is not simply shifting from one market to another but requires market research, relationship building and adaptation to individual markets’ standards and regulations, he said. 
 
 He urged businesses to strengthen their capacity to comply with rules of origin, labour and environmental requirements in order to qualify for preferential treatment, he said. 
 
 At the same time, diversification should not mean abandoning traditional markets, Khánh stressed, urging companies to pursue a balanced strategy with a clear roadmap for developing new markets while maintaining existing ones. 
 
 The government is also working to strengthen the implementation of free trade agreements, Khanh said, describing FTAs as an asset for the economy. The focus is on providing information, assessing implementation results and building an ecosystem that connects resources to help businesses make better use of FTAs, he said. 
 
 Khanh hoped Vietnam could raise its share of the CPTPP market from currently 1% to around 4-5%. 
 
 Nguyen Thi Trang, trade counsellor at the Vietnam Trade Office in Mexico, described market diversification as a long-term strategy, while stressing the importance of businesses developing their own capacity to research and build markets. 
 
 Do Thi Thuy Huong, deputy chairwoman the Vietnam Electronic Industries Association, pointed out major challenges includes access to market information, technical standards and the ability to build resilient supply chains. 
 
 Huong urged firms to adopt a more proactive approach with focus not only on responding to market demand but on actively developing markets, seeking customers and strengthening production capacity. 
 
 Such an approach would help companies turn CPTPP opportunities into sustainable export growth while building the capacity needed to participate more deeply in regional and global supply chains, she said./.

Many China tariffs remain
In February, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Trump Administration did not have the authority to unilaterally impose tariffs on imported products under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA.
IEEPA’s language does not specifically mention tariffs but does allow the president to regulate importations after declaring a national emergency. Trump had issued both reciprocal tariffs on countries which impose levies on imports from the U.S., as well as additional tariffs on China, Canada and Mexico for what he said was those governments’ failure to crack down the smuggling of fentanyl and other dangerous drugs to the U.S.
A tariff refund portal has since opened which has already returned billions of dollars in unauthorized tariffs, including nearly $1 billion to Target. However, tariffs which have been instituted under Sections 201 or 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, or Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 will remain in effect. Section 301 tariffs cover approximately 40% of U.S. imports, including many imports from China, which had an additional 12.5% tariff placed on them in July 2026.
The U.S.-China Board of Trade will be overseen by the two sides’ principals, who include Scott Bessent, secretary of the treasury, and Jamieson Greer, U.S. trade representative, on the U.S. side, and He Lifeng, vice premier of the State Council, on the Chinese side.

Coffee prices today, September 28, 2026
 World coffee prices are seeking new support amid supply pressures.
 Coffee prices have fallen across the board this past week. Robusta coffee futures contracts for November 2026 delivery on the London exchange fell 0.9% (US$29/ton) compared to the previous week, to US$3,367/ton. The January 2027 contract also fell 0.9% (US$31/ton), reaching US$3,342/ton.
 On the New York Stock Exchange, the price of Arabica coffee for December 2026 delivery fell 0.7% (1.9 US cents/pound), to 278.60 US cents/pound. The March 2027 contract fell 0.3% (0.7 US cents/pound), to 271.25 US cents/pound.
 Data from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) shows that speculators increased their short positions (betting on price declines) in ICE US arabica coffee futures contracts during the week ending September 22. Specifically, ICE coffee speculators increased their net short positions by 4,756 contracts, to 6,472 contracts.
 That's why analysts believe the current downward trend on the global market is mainly a short-term technical correction and has not yet formed a long-term recession. Once profit-taking pressure on futures exchanges subsides, combined with continued high global demand, coffee prices both domestically and internationally may soon find a short-term recovery.
 However, the prospect of increased global supply is likely to put pressure on coffee prices in the final months of the year. According to Hedgepoint Global Markets, arabica coffee is under downward pressure due to improved supply prospects, while robusta prices are supported by the potential impact of El Niño on production in Vietnam and Indonesia .
 According to the Center for Agricultural and Environmental Information and Services, Vietnam's coffee exports are projected to increase by approximately 8-10% in volume in 2026, driven by high demand for coffee that meets the EU's Anti-Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) and the rise of processed coffee, thus supporting the target of $9 billion in export value. However, coffee prices in the final months of the year may face downward pressure as global supply in the 2026/2027 crop year increases sharply and exceeds consumption demand.
 According to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), Vietnam's coffee production for the 2026-2027 crop year is projected to reach approximately 32 million bags (60 kg each), a slight increase thanks to replanted areas entering a more stable yield phase. The Vietnam Coffee and Cocoa Association also assesses the production outlook positively, but warns that El Nino and extreme weather in the Central Highlands remain significant risks to this year's coffee crop.
 Arabica coffee prices generally remain under pressure, due to expectations that Brazil has harvested a record crop in the 2026/2027 season, along with signs of increasing coffee flows from Brazil to consuming regions. In addition, brokerage firm ADMIS, a subsidiary of agricultural group Archer Daniels Midland (ADM), stated that Brazil's 2027/2028 season is also off to a good start, with abundant rainfall promoting flowering, and growing regions appearing to be receiving continued good rainfall.
 Strong actual demand is also seen as a factor providing some support to prices. Cazarini Trading Company, a Brazilian coffee brokerage firm, said in a report that if Brazil's strong export trend continues, its pessimistic view on spot coffee prices could change.
 The risk of El Niño could still impact the 2027-2028 crop cycle in Vietnam, especially as this phenomenon tends to prolong the dry season, reducing soil moisture and water resources for irrigation. Indonesia also faces the risk of impact, as crop development in its robusta-growing regions has begun. In this context, coffee prices may receive support in the coming months, depending on the extent of El Niño's impact on production in major producing countries.
 Domestic coffee prices recovered over the weekend, at one point falling to around 92,000 VND/kg, before halting their decline and returning to 93,000 - 93,800 VND/kg, the same level as the end of the previous week.
 Domestic coffee prices are moving against the global trend. An overall assessment suggests this divergence reflects the reality of supply in Vietnam, the world's largest robusta coffee exporter, which remains experiencing localized tightness. Despite a technical cooling of global prices, domestic purchasing agents are forced to raise prices to secure sufficient stock for signed export contracts. Abundant supply from Brazil and steadily increasing exports from Vietnam are putting pressure on robusta coffee prices.
 The new harvest season for Vietnamese producers and exporters is expected to officially begin next week.

Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal is likely to hold a bilateral meeting with United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer this week on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministerial in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Goyal is likely to begin his trip to the US today.
The meeting comes at a critical juncture as the US has passed a law authorising President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on India over its energy purchases from Russia.
The final decision on whether to levy the tariff, its rate and coverage, remains with Trump. The tariff threat emanates from the Lindsey O Graham Act, whilst Washington's probe against India alleging excess capacity under Section 301 of the US Trade Act is also underway.
New Delhi and Washington remain engaged in negotiations to finalise their bilateral trade deal, with India waiting for Washington to devise a mechanism ensuring competitive tariff advantages over other economies.
The Office of the USTR has already imposed a 10 per cent extra tariff on Indian goods after concluding a separate Section 301 investigation in July that claimed the involvement of forced labour in the supply chain.
Indian exporters are hopeful of clarity on India-US trade from the meetings this week, though uncertainty remains. Federation of Indian Export Organisations Director General Ajay Sahai noted that the delegation is expected to flag New Delhi's concerns.
Both sides had proposed the bilateral trade agreement last year in February and issued a joint statement on the first tranche this year in February, agreeing on a lower reciprocal tariff of 18 per cent for Indian goods.

articles.title: Beyond Nearshoring: The Regionalization Challenge - Mexico Business News
articles.summary: Beyond Nearshoring: The Regionalization Challenge  Mexico Business News
articles.full_text:
For the past several years, nearshoring has dominated Mexico’s industrial conversation. We have discussed new factories, industrial parks, investment announcements, and the relocation of global supply chains closer to the United States.
Those indicators matter. But after experiencing this transformation from several perspectives — as a manufacturing CEO, president of INDEX Nuevo Leon, professor at Tecnológico de Monterrey, and through my participation in the Tier 2 Committee of CLAUT, Nuevo León’s automotive cluster — I have become convinced that the next industrial challenge is fundamentally different.
Mexico must move from nearshoring to regionalization. Attracting a factory is an investment decision. Building a competitive regional supply chain is an industrial transformation.
The distinction matters.
A multinational company may establish a plant in Mexico while continuing to import a significant portion of its materials, components, tooling and technology from outside North America. The investment has been nearshored, but the supply chain has not necessarily been regionalized.
The next frontier is therefore not simply attracting more manufacturing. It is increasing the amount of value that Mexico, the United States, and Canada can collectively produce inside North America.
The scale of the opportunity is enormous. US-Mexico trade in goods and services reached an estimated US$964.1 billion in 2025. Mexico remains deeply integrated with the US industrial economy, particularly in automotive, electronics, medical devices and advanced manufacturing. The question is no longer whether this integration exists. The question is how much deeper and more strategic it can become.
From Locating Suppliers to Developing Them
This challenge becomes particularly visible when working with Tier 2 companies.
Large manufacturers do not select suppliers simply because they are geographically closer. A regional supplier must demonstrate competitive cost, quality systems, capacity, delivery performance, financial stability, traceability, and the ability to operate under global manufacturing standards.
That experience has shaped one of the initiatives we have developed at INDEX Nuevo León: PROCIM (Proveedor Confiable para la Industria Manufacturera).
Its deliberate underlying premise is that the supply chain does not need another supplier directory. It needs trust.
PROCIM seeks to move beyond simply identifying suppliers toward building more reliable connections between manufacturing companies and potential regional suppliers that have gone through an initial administrative pre-screening process. At the same time, PROCIM seeks to help regional suppliers better understand industry requirements, strengthen their capabilities and become more competitive. This distinction is important: regionalization requires not only greater visibility between buyers and suppliers, but also stronger capabilities and a better understanding of what global manufacturers require before considering new sourcing relationships.
Regionalization cannot simply mean asking companies to “buy Mexican.” It must mean developing regional suppliers capable of winning business on merit.
Talent Is Also Part of the Supply Chain
Regionalization, however, cannot be solved through procurement alone.
As a professor at Tecnológico de Monterrey, I see another side of the equation: the people who will operate, improve, and eventually redesign these supply chains.
Through the Tec21 educational model, students work with companies on real business challenges. That experience reinforces something industry sometimes overlooks: universities should not operate adjacent to the manufacturing ecosystem. They should be part of it.
Engineers, technicians, supply-chain professionals, data specialists, and future business leaders are becoming strategic infrastructure.
Machines can be purchased. Buildings can be constructed. Capital can cross borders quickly.
Capabilities take years to develop.
This is why collaboration among companies, universities, clusters, and industry associations will become increasingly important.
The Tier 2 Opportunity
My participation in CLAUT’s Tier 2 Committee has reinforced the same conclusion from another perspective.
Mexico has built an extraordinary automotive manufacturing base. But the next level of competitiveness will depend increasingly on what happens deeper in the supply chain.
Tier 2 and Tier 3 companies represent one of Mexico’s greatest opportunities for increasing regional content. Developing them means strengthening technical capabilities, quality systems, automation, digitalization, access to talent, and connections with larger manufacturers.
This challenge is particularly relevant in Nuevo Leon. The state closed 2025 with 394,206 jobs associated with the IMMEX program, the highest total in Mexico. The significance of that number extends beyond employment. It reflects the density of an industrial ecosystem capable of becoming a laboratory for the next phase of regional integration.
From Mexican Competitiveness to North American Competitiveness
This also changes the way we should think about USMCA.
The agreement should not be viewed merely as a framework governing trade among three countries. It can become the architecture for building one of the world’s most competitive manufacturing regions.
That evolution is already entering the bilateral agenda. Discussions surrounding the USMCA review have increasingly focused on expanding North American manufacturing, strengthening regional supply chains, and reducing dependence on nonmarket inputs from outside the region.
The United States contributes extraordinary innovation, technology, and capital. Canada provides advanced industrial capabilities, energy, and natural resources. Mexico contributes manufacturing depth, engineering talent, and an increasingly sophisticated supplier ecosystem.
The opportunity lies in connecting those strengths more deliberately.
The question for the coming decade should therefore evolve from, “How much investment can Mexico attract?,” to “How much North American value can we create together?”
For Nuevo Leon, this transition is already tangible. Through INDEX, manufacturing companies, supplier-development initiatives such as PROCIM, automotive clusters, and universities, I see different institutions confronting different pieces of the same challenge.
What is missing is not opportunity. What we need is greater connection among those pieces.
Nearshoring brought the world’s attention back to Mexico. Regionalization can transform that attention into something far more durable: deeper supply chains, stronger suppliers, better jobs, greater technological capability, and a more competitive North American industrial platform.
Mexico’s next industrial chapter should therefore not be measured only by the factories we attract, but by the capabilities we build around them.
Mexico’s opportunity is no longer simply to manufacture more. It is to become the place where North America integrates, innovates, and competes.

articles.full_text:
TORONTO (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. owner of steelmaker Stelco, a subsidiary of Cleveland-Cliffs, of betraying Canadian workers Tuesday after it announced layoffs it attributed in part to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs — tariffs Cleveland-Cliffs’ chief executive has publicly championed.
Carney singled out Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves, noting that he had applauded Trump’s steel tariffs. Goncalves has called the 50% tariffs “a necessary step” to protect U.S. steelmakers.
“Our thoughts are with the workers and the families who have been betrayed by the company,” Carney said.
Carney also threatened legal action against Cleveland-Cliffs, saying the Ohio-based company has binding employment obligations stemming from its C$3.4 billion ($2.4 billion) takeover of Stelco in 2024.
Stelco said up to 500 workers could be affected as it indefinitely idles cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant and shifts production to its Lake Erie facility in Nanticoke, Ontario.
Cleveland-Cliffs said Monday the move does not shift steel production out of Canada: Output will be concentrated at Stelco’s Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ontario, where it expects a significant number of affected Hamilton workers to be absorbed, with overall steel tonnage unchanged.
In a memo to employees, Stelco said U.S. tariffs had “significantly shrunk the market” for its cold-rolled and galvanized products. The company said demand in markets it traditionally serves fell almost 25% in the second quarter compared to the 2024 quarterly average, including a 10% decline in Canada.
The layoffs come amid an escalating Canada-U.S. trade war in which Trump has imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian steel and other goods and Canada has retaliated with tariffs of its own. At a White House event Monday announcing a new $15 billion steel plant in Iowa, Trump credited his tariffs with reducing foreign steel imports and attracting investment to the United States, saying companies were building plants there “because they don’t want to pay tariffs.”
Carney said the federal government had offered financial assistance to preserve jobs but did not disclose the amount or terms.
“There’s money on the table from the federal government,” Carney said. “The company made representations and has legal obligations for employment. We intend to use all powers that we have and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law.”
The Canadian government approved Cleveland-Cliffs’ takeover of Stelco in October 2024 on the condition that it meet legally binding five-year employment commitments, including maintaining at least the same number of unionized workers and the vast majority of nonunion employees.
Cleveland-Cliffs did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Carney’s remarks.
